questions.question: Explain how differential erosion in horizontal strata builds the landform family of the Karoo, naming each member of the family in its correct erosional order with a South African example.
questions.expected_answer: The Karoo Supergroup is a thick pile of flat-lying mudstones, shales and sandstones intruded by resistant dolerite sills about one hundred and eighty-three million years ago. Because the layers are unequal in resistance, weathering and erosion strip the weak layers quickly while the strong ones survive — differential erosion. A resistant cap rock shields the soft strata beneath it, so a protected surface stays high and flat with steep sides. The sequence runs: plateau, a broad elevated surface edged by an escarpment; mesa, a detached flat-topped remnant still broader than it is tall, called a tafelberg; butte, the same body narrowed until it is taller than it is broad with a small flat crown — Teebus and Koffiebus near Steynsburg show the mesa and butte forms side by side; conical hill, formed once the cap is breached and the exposed soft strata weather into a smooth cone, as at Spandau Kop outside Graaff-Reinet; and finally the plain. The Lesotho highlands are the igneous version — stacked horizontal basalt lava flows forming a basaltic plateau.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of scarp retreat, distinguish back wasting from down wasting, and explain how pediments grow into a pediplain.
questions.expected_answer: The cliff below the cap is attacked on two fronts: in winter, water freezing in the joints of the dolerite expands and levers blocks off the face, while summer thunderstorms scour the weak shale beneath the cap so the unsupported cap blocks collapse. The cliff is therefore rebuilt at the same steep angle a little further back after each cycle — the slope retreats parallel to itself, which is scarp retreat or parallel retreat, the model Lester King developed on South African landscapes. Back wasting is erosion in this style, slopes migrating sideways while holding their shape; down wasting is the opposite, the lowering of a landscape from the top so summits sink and profiles round off. Capped strata resist down wasting because the cap locks the summit height, forcing all yield inward from the edges. Each retreating scarp leaves a gently inclined bedrock surface at its foot, the pediment; when scarps retreating from opposite sides of an upland finally meet, their pediments merge into a vast, almost level erosion surface — the pediplain, of which the Great Karoo is the standing example, scattered with surviving mesas, buttes and cones.

questions.question: Describe how canyons form in horizontal strata with named examples, and show how this terrain is handled in mapwork: contour signatures, vertical exaggeration and gradient, with full working.
questions.expected_answer: A large, energetic river attacking horizontal strata saws directly downward, cutting a canyon — a deep, narrow valley with near-vertical walls that descend in giant steps because each resistant band stands as a sheer face while each weak band wears back into a slope. The Grand Canyon of the Colorado is the world's classic and the Blyde River Canyon on the Mpumalanga escarpment, sunk some eight hundred metres into layered quartzites, is South Africa's showpiece; uplift that rejuvenates the river deepens the cut. On the map, a mesa shows as closed contours with a strikingly empty summit ringed by tightly bunched contours marking the cliff; a butte gives the same signature with a tiny summit; stepped slopes alternate crowded and spaced contour bands; a canyon shows as two parallel ribbons of packed contours with the river squeezed between. Vertical exaggeration divides the vertical scale by the horizontal scale: a vertical scale of one centimetre to twenty-five metres is 1:2 500, so against 1:50 000 the exaggeration is 50 000 divided by 2 500, which is 20 times. Gradient is height difference over horizontal distance in the same units: a climb of 150 metres over 3 000 metres is 150 over 3 000, which is 1 in 20.
